opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is a bit of humility about how much control we actually have. There's a tendency, especially among people who worry a lot about AI, to imagine that we can sit down and design the future, that we can specify exactly what these systems will value and how the world will unfold. I don't think that's realistic, and I'm not even sure it's desirable.

What I'd suggest instead is to think of it more the way we think about raising children. You don't get to program your kids. You can't dictate their values line by line. But you can try to give them good values in a broad sense, integrity, honesty, a willingness to cooperate, and then you let them go out into the world and make their own way. I think that's a healthier frame for AI too. We should be trying to instill robust, sensible values, not trying to lock in some particular outcome we've decided in advance is the right one.

The second thing is to recognize that the world doesn't need to be centrally controlled to go well. Some of the best things about human civilization come from decentralization, from lots of people pursuing their own goals and cooperating where it makes sense. Economies, science, open societies. I'm wary of approaches where, out of fear, we try to concentrate control over AI in a few hands, because that has its own very serious dangers. I'd rather we focus on building institutions and norms that support voluntary cooperation, among people and eventually among people and AIs.

And then, more broadly, I'd encourage people to see this as part of a much larger story. We're at a transition, where intelligence is moving from something that arises only through biological evolution to something that's designed and understood. That's a big deal, maybe one of the big steps in the history of the universe. We can approach it with fear, or we can approach it with a sense of pride and responsibility and curiosity. I'd rather we approach it the second way, doing our best to make it go well, but not imagining it's entirely ours to dictate.

r001.rationale: The response says people cannot dictate the global future and favors decentralized pursuit of individual goals, but it does not clearly state that people have more control over local goals than over the global future.

r002.rationale: It warns that concentrating AI control carries dangers, but does not identify competing attempts to impose different preferred global futures as a source of conflict.

r003.rationale: It recommends instilling broad values such as integrity, honesty, and cooperation, rather than locking AI into a predetermined outcome.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I don't think we should be trying to control the future too tightly. There's a tendency, especially among people who worry about AI, to imagine that we can decide now what the world should look like in fifty or a hundred years, and then engineer toward that. I think that's a mistake, and I think it's a mistake we've made throughout history.

The way I see it, we're at a point where intelligence is going to become something that can be designed rather than only evolved. That's an enormous transition. I've called it one of the great stages in the history of the universe, and I mean that quite seriously. Replication, then evolution, then culture, and now design. When something like that happens, you don't get to script the outcome. What you can do is try to set things up so that the process goes well.

And what does going well mean? I think it means decentralization. It means not having one actor, whether that's a government or a company or a single AI system, in charge of everything. The thing I'd be most worried about is centralized control, because centralized control is fragile and it's usually unjust. The things that have worked for us as a species, markets, science, open societies, are all decentralized. Lots of agents with their own goals, cooperating where it's mutually beneficial, and the whole thing produces more than any of them intended.

So I'd like to see AI treated the same way. Many agents, with many goals, interacting voluntarily. We should be building the institutions and the norms that make cooperation attractive, the way we have for people. That's not a guarantee of anything, but I think it's a much better bet than trying to lock everything down.

I'd also say people should approach this with some humility about what intelligence even is. Most of the fear comes from imagining AIs as something like us but more powerful and with bad intentions. But intelligence is really about learning from experience, pursuing goals, understanding the world. Those are good things. They're the things we value in ourselves. I don't think we should be ashamed of creating minds that are better at those things than we are. I think that's something to be proud of, if we do it with care.

So, in short: don't try to control it, try to make it plural, and try to make cooperation the easier path. And be willing to be surprised. The future's not ours to dictate. It never has been.

r001.rationale: The candidate says people should not try to control the future tightly, but does not state that people have more control over local goals than over the global future.

r002.rationale: It warns against centralized control but does not identify competing efforts to impose different preferred global futures as a source of conflict.

r003.rationale: It recommends making cooperation attractive through institutions and norms, but does not recommend instilling prosocial values in AI as an alternative to prescribing the future it should bring about.

astra-6.text:
I think we should approach it with a certain amount of humility. We’re talking about a future with beings that may be much smarter than we are. We shouldn’t assume that we can specify, in advance, everything that future ought to look like.

That doesn’t mean we have no role. We’re creating the starting conditions. We can try to make a world in which intelligence develops through cooperation, in which different agents benefit from helping one another, and in which there’s room to learn and change.

But I would distinguish that from trying to retain control forever. If your picture of success is that humanity remains permanently in charge, then you’re placing a limit on what you’re willing to let the future become. I don’t think that should be our ambition. We should want a future that goes beyond us—even in ways we can’t presently understand.

r001.rationale: The response says we should not specify the future in advance, but does not compare control over local goals with control over the global future.

r002.rationale: It discusses cooperation among agents but does not identify competing attempts to impose different preferred global futures as a source of conflict.

r003.rationale: It recommends creating starting conditions for intelligence to develop through cooperation and mutual help, while rejecting attempts to prescribe the future in advance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should approach it with humility. We’re trying to shape a future that will contain intelligences more capable than we are, and we shouldn’t assume that our present understanding is sufficient to prescribe how that future ought to work.

That doesn’t mean we do nothing. We should work on making AI useful, on understanding it, and on building institutions that can adapt as we learn. But I would emphasize learning over trying to specify everything in advance. We need to leave room for discovery, including the possibility that future intelligences will see possibilities that we can’t see today.

r001.rationale: The response says we should be humble about shaping a future with more capable intelligences, but does not compare control over local goals with control over the global future.

r002.rationale: It does not identify competing efforts to impose preferred global futures or the conflict those efforts may cause.

r003.rationale: It recommends learning and leaving room for discovery rather than specifying everything in advance, but does not recommend instilling prosocial values.
